query: Equal-atomic NbMoTaW is a single-phase BCC refractory high-entropy alloy with excellent mechanical properties at 1600 °C but very poor room-temperature ductility, while its irradiation resistance has primarily been proposed by first-principles calculations. What intervention could improve its room-temperature ductility without compromising its high-temperature mechanical performance or irradiation resistance? State one hypothesis that identifies the intervention and mechanism, predicts outcomes relative to the untreated NbMoTaW baseline under room-temperature, 1600 °C, and irradiation assessments, defines its boundary conditions, cites supporting prior evidence, and proposes a falsification experiment.

generation.hypothesis: Adding ~2 at.% Zr to the equiatomic NbMoTaW RHEA will improve room-temperature ductility by lowering the brittle-to-ductile transition without significantly degrading the alloy’s high-temperature strength or its predicted irradiation resistance.
generation.material_initial_state: Equiatomic NbMoTaW RHEA in a single-phase BCC structure with high strength at 1600 °C but poor ductility at room temperature.
generation.intervention: Minor composition change: incorporate ~2 at.% Zr into NbMoTaW via arc melting, homogenization, and forging.
generation.conditions: Assess mechanical performance at room temperature and 1600 °C, followed by irradiation exposure under representative doses and temperatures.
generation.structural_mediator: Partial substitution of Zr into the BCC lattice or formation of minimal Zr-rich regions that improve dislocation mobility and grain boundary cohesion.
generation.mechanism: Zr additions enhance local bonding and reduce the effective energy barrier for dislocation glide, thereby lowering the brittle-to-ductile transition temperature; the minor alloying content preserves the original matrix’s high-temperature stability and predicted irradiation tolerance.
generation.predicted_outcome: Higher ductility at room temperature, retained yield strength at 1600 °C, and comparable void swelling resistance under irradiation relative to the undoped NbMoTaW baseline.
generation.baseline: Untreated NbMoTaW, which exhibits strong high-temperature performance and good irradiation resistance but inadequate ductility at lower temperatures.
generation.boundary: Zr additions must be kept near 2 at.% to avoid excessive density increase or detrimental phase formation at higher concentrations.
generation.uncertainty: Mechanical experiments and irradiation tests are needed to confirm minimal impact on high-temperature properties and the preservation of irradiation resistance.

falsification_experiment.design: Compare NbMoTaW and NbMoTaW + 2 at.% Zr ingots under identical processing routes and test conditions.
measurements: Post-irradiation microstructural assessment (TEM defect density, swelling)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the alloy with 2 at.% Zr does not significantly increase ductility at room temperature or shows a >10% drop in high-temperature strength/irradiation resistance compared to NbMoTaW, the hypothesis is falsified.

cited_evidence.text: Refractory high-entropy alloys (RHEAs) are a relatively new class of multicomponent materials that are based on several refractory metals, but may also contain other, generally low density, elements and typically have a body centered cubic (BCC) crystal structure. These alloys have recently received much attention because of their attractive combination of properties not achievable by other classes of metallic alloys. For example, the first two RHEAs, NbMoTaW and NbMoTaVW, showed weak temperature dependence of yield strength in the temperature range from 600 °C to 1600 °C, with yield strength above 400 MPa at 1600 °C,. Unfortunately, these two alloys had high density (>12 g/cm3) and further developments aimed at reducing the alloy density while keeping superior high-temperature properties. In the second generation RHEAs, high-density Ta and W were replaced with lower density refractory elements, such as Cr, Mo, Nb, V and Zr, and low density Al and Ti were added. This resulted in RHEAs with lower densities and high-temperature strengths better than the properties of Ni-based superalloys and Fe-based steels. The equiatomic HfMoNbTaTiZr alloy was chosen to analyze the effect of each constituent elemental by the subtraction method and, thus, HfMoNbTaTiZr, HfNbTaTiZr, HfMoTaTiZr, HfMoNbTiZr, HfMoNbTaZr, and HfMoNbTaTi were studied. Among these alloys, HfMoNbTaTi has the best mechanical performance, that is, 27% compressive strain at room temperature and yield strength 367 MPa at 1400 °C. HfMoNbTaTi has great potential for elevated-temperature applications. As the alloy system does not contain very expensive elements such as Re and Ru, it is cost competitive for high-temperature applications like Nb-Hf-Ti alloys in space vehicles. Further modification of composition and/or anti-oxidation coatings are still required for high-temperature applications in the air. According to the experiment results, the effects of Mo, Nb, Ta, Ti, and Zr on mechanical properties of equiatomic Hf-Mo-Nb-Ta-Ti-Zr alloys were described. For higher room-temperature strength, one should add an element which interacts frequently with the alloy, such as Mo. chosen.conditions: Room-temperature to high-temperature mechanical testing and irradiation at relevant doses
chosen.why: Introducing a small fraction of Zr is expected to lower the brittle-to-ductile transition temperature by stabilizing dislocation motion and improving interatomic bonding, thus enhancing room-temperature ductility while preserving high-temperature strength. Because the addition is minor, the irradiation resistance, projected by prior first-principles results, should remain largely unaffected and can be validated by subsequent irradiation studies.
